title: Max Junestrand, Legora: 'We're Setting the Precedent'
author: Richard Tromans · Max Junestrand

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not directly address the cluster’s central apprenticeship and verification paradox. It instead shifts attention to the people and workflow investment needed for adoption, and to how AI may reduce associate-heavy leverage and reshape pricing for specialist expertise.
qs: And there’s a tremendous amount of work and energy and time that needs to go in to how to empower your teams to get the most out of AI.

I think Richard, you’re completely right in the observation that AI is an unlock for really talented people with sort of deep and narrow expertise to maybe start their own firms, which hasn’t been, it hasn’t been possible before because you’re going to get the leverage and you know, the leverage on a law firm was like you, you, you, you build a lot of associate hours.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Junestrand does not directly address error propagation or verification bottlenecks, but materially extends the cluster’s implementation argument: capable AI must be paired with substantial team enablement and lawyer-led workflow redesign. His prediction that one-prompt perfect drafting remains distant also reinforces the cluster’s caution against equating model capability with autonomous legal delivery.
qs: And there’s a tremendous amount of work and energy and time that needs to go in to how to empower your teams to get the most out of AI.

They come in with a mindset that’s like, I used to know how it was practicing in this practice area, and now with AI, we can totally reshape the way that work gets done.** And we want to help figure that out.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Junestrand accepts that model capability alone is insufficient and materially develops the cluster’s implementation argument: complex legal work requires specialist products, substantial adoption effort, expert legal engineers and workflow redesign. His account supports this through development and deployment experience, not comparative performance evidence, and does not directly establish broader reliability or autonomous end-to-end work.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source accepts that in-house AI demand can shift work toward client self-service, then materially extends the cluster by proposing a collaborative, firm-branded model: law firms package their workflows, templates and playbooks for clients while preserving the advisory relationship. This supports selective insourcing without assuming universal outside-counsel decline, though the claimed demand and relationship benefits are not quantified.
qs: And I think that’s a real opportunity for the law firms to offer a white-labeled  firm specific product to those clients and then go, that’s awesome that you also want to start using AI.
And so we want to build the software, the vessel, the solution to that problem so that they can retain that client relationship and deliver that work in a 2025 way.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Junestrand accepts that AI adoption is a business-model and competitive-positioning problem, then materially extends the cluster by predicting AI-related scale benefits, law-firm consolidation and hybrid organisational structures. His account also reinforces the need for providers to choose where they compete and how much of the value chain they seek to capture, although these claims are based on industry conversations rather than quantified outcomes.
qs: Law firms will be buying law firms because there’ll be new types of sort of scale benefits when it comes to how you can deliver this in effective ways, how you can proactively have the conversations with the clients, how you can use your data, how you can turn your work into AI processes.
I think the question the law firms and the legal service providers have to ask themselves is, where do we want to play?

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI capability alone does not create value and materially develops the institutional-absorption proposition by identifying intensive team enablement and an experienced legal-engineering function as mechanisms for redesigning legal workflows. Its support rests on reported deployment experience rather than measured outcomes.
qs: And there’s a tremendous amount of work and energy and time that needs to go in to how to empower your teams to get the most out of AI.

They come in with a mindset that’s like, I used to know how it was practicing in this practice area, and now with AI, we can totally reshape the way that work gets done.** And we want to help figure that out.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Junestrand accepts that AI pressures production economics more than the continuing value of lawyers, especially by compressing associate hours while scarce partner expertise remains valuable. He materially extends the cluster with concrete proposals for alternative fees, firm-branded self-service workflows, AI-oriented organisational structures and legal-engineering investment, while acknowledging present technical limits.
qs: And if we want to keep that work, we likely need to find an alternative fee arrangement to be able to deliver it in a smart way and in a competitive way.
And I think that’s a real opportunity for the law firms to offer a white-labeled  firm specific product to those clients and then go, that’s awesome that you also want to start using AI.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Legora accepts the cluster’s core framing of AI adoption as organisational and workflow redesign rather than a software purchase. It materially extends that proposition with a concrete implementation model: investing substantial time and support in adoption and deploying experienced legal engineers to reshape practice-area workflows. Its business-model observations also reinforce the cluster’s account of incentive-based resistance, though outcomes remain company-reported rather than measured.
qs: And there’s a tremendous amount of work and energy and time that needs to go in to how to empower your teams to get the most out of AI.

They come in with a mindset that’s like, I used to know how it was practicing in this practice area, and now with AI, we can totally reshape the way that work gets done.** And we want to help figure that out.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Junestrand accepts the cluster’s core view that current legal AI is task-bounded and that value depends on organisational redesign rather than model access alone. He materially extends it with a concrete enterprise-delivery model centred on practice-specific legal engineering, scalable infrastructure, deliberate user experience and redesigned client workflows, while linking those changes to pricing and leverage pressures.
qs: They come in with a mindset that’s like, I used to know how it was practicing in this practice area, and now with AI, we can totally reshape the way that work gets done.** And we want to help figure that out.

And also, I mean, **what I think sometimes can get overlooked is just the amount of enterprise features and product that’s required to scale these systems to, know, tens, multiple tens of thousands of users every day**.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: Junestrand accepts the cluster’s view that AI-enabled delivery will favour differentiated operating models and strategic work segmentation. He materially extends it by predicting AI- and data-driven scale benefits will spur law-firm consolidation and by identifying partnership-owned corporate subsidiaries as a possible structure for AI-oriented work, while treating these outcomes as prospective rather than established.
qs: Law firms will be buying law firms because there’ll be new types of sort of scale benefits when it comes to how you can deliver this in effective ways, how you can proactively have the conversations with the clients, how you can use your data, how you can turn your work into AI processes.

Increasingly, I’ve also heard firms considering in the UK especially  Can we have a subsidiary that’s a corporate that’s kind of owned by the partnership that can do some of this other work that will sort of be more AI-esque in nature, right?

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Junestrand supports the synthesis’s core view that AI will pressure hourly pricing and require strategic redesign of legal delivery rather than simple task automation. He also reinforces the implementation bottleneck by stressing investment in people, legal engineering and new workflows, while treating productivity and consolidation claims as pilot-based or prospective. He does not materially address verification or the apprenticeship and succession problem.
qs: And if we want to keep that work, we likely need to find an alternative fee arrangement to be able to deliver it in a smart way and in a competitive way.
And there’s a tremendous amount of work and energy and time that needs to go in to how to empower your teams to get the most out of AI.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Junestrand supports the proposition that improving general models broaden legal AI’s capabilities while leaving durable value in specialist workflow products. He presents Legora’s expanding application suite, client-shaped roadmap and lawyer-led legal engineering as necessary complements to foundation models, and says fully autonomous, perfect contract generation remains distant. His support rests on company experience and self-reported adoption rather than independent testing.
qs: We decided very clearly that like….the models are going to keep improving and the products that you can build on top of this is going to expand very quickly.
And **we’ve deployed a huge legal engineering team** that only focus on this.

st.t: Legora expansion: Workflow usefulness must sustain global scale
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by attributing Legora’s rapid international growth to focused product execution, an expanding workflow suite and client-developed roadmaps rather than first-mover status. It also confirms centralised engineering and short planning cycles. Its growth and success claims remain company-reported and provide no independent measurement of legal-work improvement.
qs: **What’s exciting for me is that this product roadmap is being created sort of as we go together with our clients because AI is new to everyone**.
And so, as we’ll maybe get to like, yes, like Legora was not the first player in this space, but we have executed with an enormous amount of focus and emphasis on product.

kp.k: Legora reports rapid enterprise adoption and global expansion
kp.d: Junestrand reports $265 million raised, growth from a few customers to over 550 following general availability in October 2024, and workforce expansion from 40 to well over 220 during 2025. He says the company is set to more than double its workforce the following year. These are company-reported figures and plans, not independently assessed adoption or productivity findings.
qs: And I think to date, we’ve raised $265 million, which sounds like a really big number.
we only launched in sort of general availability in October, 2024.
And so in that very short period of time, we’ve scaled from a couple of customers to over 550.
So we’ve scaled this year alone from 40 to well over 220. And next year we’re set to more than double that.

kp.k: Legal AI products are becoming integrated suites
kp.d: Junestrand describes Legora's development from a chat interface into a suite incorporating Portal, tabular review and office-software integrations, with a mobile app forthcoming. He argues that connecting functions creates capabilities unavailable in separate systems. The roadmap is developed with clients, while Legora interprets general-purpose models and frameworks for legal work.
qs: the first version of Legora was really like a chat GPT-esque interface. And now it’s so much more. It’s an entire suite.
What’s exciting for me is that this product roadmap is being created sort of as we go together with our clients because AI is new to everyone
So it’s actually about bundling it all together and providing the lawyer with a single user interface that can do more and more things every single week.

kp.k: Enterprise implementation requires services and local support
kp.d: Junestrand argues that enterprise deployment requires local expertise and assistance with changes to working practices and business organisation, rather than software distribution alone. He links global offices to supporting clients such as Linklaters and describes the Indian operation as providing legal engineering, customer success and support. Core product engineering remains in Stockholm, with a stated commitment against outsourcing engineering.
qs: I think it’s important to note that the product is one thing, but there’s an enormous amount of service around the product when you implement Legora
we want to be able to support them on site with legal engineers, with customer success, with support.
So we will never outsource engineering

kp.d: Junestrand presents Portal as a collaborative environment intended to replace fragmented email exchanges and let clients use law-firm workflows, templates and playbooks. Although it works in both directions, the initial focus is law firms offering white-labelled products to in-house clients, preserving relationships as tasks become automatable. Tromans challenges the claim of unprecedented innovation by mentioning HighQ; Junestrand distinguishes Portal's workflows and self-service from what he characterises as HighQ's static file sharing.
qs: Well, it actually works both ways. But we’re very much focused and sort of initially focused on the law firms.
By the way, we already have created these workflows, these templates, these playbooks that you can self serve on.
so that they can retain that client relationship and deliver that work in a 2025 way.
Well, I mean, I don’t know, I mean, I suppose HighQ and others might disagree a little bit.

kp.k: Automation pressures firms toward alternative fee arrangements
kp.d: Junestrand predicts that AI will handle increasingly complex tasks, while qualifying that it does not yet address all work. He argues that providers wishing to retain automatable work will likely need alternative fee arrangements and that proactive firms will fare better than those changing only under client pressure. This is a strategic prediction rather than evidence that hourly billing has already disappeared.
qs: AI is not a silver bullet for every task and for everything yet.
And if we want to keep that work, we likely need to find an alternative fee arrangement to be able to deliver it in a smart way and in a competitive way.
I think firms who lead with this proactively versus reactively when they get pushed by their clients, I think we’ll have much more success in the market.

kp.k: Pilot time savings prompt a value-pricing discussion
kp.d: Junestrand reports that some product-comparison pilots found a task previously taking six hours took 20 minutes. He argues that reduced time does not necessarily reduce client value and identifies pricing as a difficult transition. No task specification, sample size, methodology or quality assessment accompanies this anecdotal productivity claim.
qs: they have findings like we used to spend six hours on this thing and now it takes 20 minutes.
However, is the value that they’re providing any less? No.
And the client was willing to pay something much bigger than 20 minutes times the hourly rate.

kp.k: AI may reshape provider structures and expertise pricing
kp.d: Junestrand says partnership and corporate models suit different work and reports hearing UK firms consider corporate subsidiaries for more AI-oriented services. He argues that AI enables specialists to establish firms and challenges a revenue model built around associate hours. He suggests repricing scarce partner expertise that AI cannot supply; Tromans separately criticises billing junior hours when much of the value resides in experienced partners.
qs: The corporate model, you know, sort of scale up model fits some work well too.
Can we have a subsidiary that’s a corporate that’s kind of owned by the partnership that can do some of this other work that will sort of be more AI-esque in nature, right?
the leverage on a law firm was like you, you, you, you build a lot of associate hours. Like that’s how you make money.

when you need the partner for something that AI absolutely cannot do and for something that, you know, nobody else in the firm really knows, it’s worth a lot more than that sort of number they put on it.

kp.k: New scale benefits could drive law-firm consolidation
kp.d: Junestrand predicts winners, losers, ranking shifts and acquisitions among law firms. His proposed mechanism is new scale advantages in efficient delivery, proactive client discussions, data use and conversion of legal work into AI processes. He describes these issues as frequent topics with legal-service leaders but supplies no measured consolidation evidence or specific forecast horizon.
qs: And I think they’ll be winners and losers. And I think this is a time and a place where rankings can shift or will shift.
There will be consolidation in the legal market.
how you can use your data, how you can turn your work into AI processes.

kp.k: Rapid model change shortens operational planning
kp.d: Junestrand says Legora plans approximately one quarter ahead while retaining longer-term roadmap initiatives. Its functionality is designed to benefit from improving underlying models. When Tromans proposes a future market dominated by LexisNexis, Thomson Reuters, Legora, Harvey and Clio, Junestrand does not endorse that forecast: he stresses five-year uncertainty and expresses a conditional ambition to rank first.
qs: at Legora, we don’t do yearly planning
We plan for about one quarter ahead.
And we build all our functionality like boats so that they sort of improve when the tide rises.
And so I think it’s really hard to say what the ecosystem is going to look like in five years.
Well, if it was up to a top five, we’d love to be number one.

kp.k: Model capability exceeds current products and user adoption
kp.d: Asked whether LLM improvements are plateauing, Junestrand argues there remains substantial scope to translate existing capabilities into legal products through scaffolding and other techniques. He explicitly says obtaining a perfect share purchase agreement from a simple prompt is not currently possible and may remain distant. His response locates immediate constraints in product development and adoption rather than demonstrating a model-performance trend.
qs: So we’re not yet running into constraints because there’s so much left to build and there’s so many sort of scaffolding and techniques that you can use to get more juice out of the models.
Of course it would be great like you just throw a prompt at GPT, like write me a share purchase agreement and you get the perfect output. But we’re not there.

kp.k: Legal engineers support changes in lawyers' working practices
kp.d: Junestrand emphasises the time and effort required to teach teams new ways of working, comparing adoption to learning Excel or riding a bicycle. He reports deploying a large legal engineering team, including lawyers from Kirkland, Cooley, Baker McKenzie and Bird & Bird, to help reshape practice-area workflows. This describes vendor-led adoption support, not evidence of changes to formal legal qualification or junior training systems.
qs: Just because the product can do amazing things, or just because the models can do amazing things, you need to get the people there.
we’ve deployed a huge legal engineering team

And these are excellent lawyers coming from firms like Kirkland, Cooley, Baker McKenzie, Bird & Bird. They come in with a mindset that’s like, I used to know how it was practicing in this practice area, and now with AI, we can totally reshape the way that work gets done.

kp.k: Enterprise design differentiates platforms from do-it-yourself tools
kp.d: Tromans argues that reproducing a feature with a public model overlooks ongoing engineering, design and product-management requirements. Junestrand adds enterprise-scale operation, integrated functionality, deliberately designed user experience and early access to models through AI-lab relationships. These are arguments for buying a maintained platform, not comparative cost or performance findings.
qs: there’s so much more than just being able to just jump onto an LLM.
what I think sometimes can get overlooked is just the amount of enterprise features and product that’s required to scale these systems to, know, tens, multiple tens of thousands of users every day
You want a designer to have really thought about how to make usability and user experience the best for your type of users.

kp.k: Founder control and fundraising support long-term vendor strategy
kp.d: Junestrand reports that founders hold three board seats against investors' two, framing this as protection against short-term targets compromising the business or mission. He says investors have long holding horizons and describes the last two fundraising rounds as market-signalling exercises rather than responses to funding need. These are his account of governance and financing motives.
qs: So me and my co-founder, we have three seats and the investors have two seats in the current setup.
They’re not investors that are pushing us to sell or go public to sell their stocks.
the last two runs of fundraise that we’ve done was not because we needed the money. It’s to make sure that the market knows that we’re doing really well.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Junestrand predicts expanding automation of increasingly complex legal tasks, but does not claim that AI can presently perform all legal work.
pts.d: He describes a trajectory from summarisation toward more complex tasks and treats automation of technically solvable tasks as inevitable. This concerns law firms and other legal service providers deciding which work to retain. His expectation is open-ended rather than attached to a completion date, and he explicitly qualifies present capabilities.

pts.k: Junestrand argues that AI time savings create pressure to replace hourly billing with alternative fee arrangements, with proactive firms more likely to succeed.
pts.d: For work AI can perform, he says providers wishing to retain that work will likely need alternative fee arrangements to remain competitive. He reports pilot findings in which a task fell from six hours to 20 minutes and argues that the value delivered did not fall correspondingly. He predicts winners, losers and changes in firm rankings as providers navigate pricing. The pilot example is a speaker-reported finding, not a documented benchmark; no task description, sample, quality assessment or verification-time breakdown is supplied.

pts.k: Junestrand predicts law-firm consolidation driven by new AI-related economies of scale.
pts.d: He expects firms to acquire other firms because of advantages in efficient delivery, client engagement, data use and converting existing work into AI processes. He frames these changes as already developing, but supplies no acquisition examples, estimates of scale benefits or forecast horizon. His stated basis is frequent discussions with legal service leaders.

pts.k: Junestrand claims that AI enables specialist-led firms and alternative organisational arrangements while making exceptional partner expertise more important to price explicitly.
pts.d: He argues that deeply specialised practitioners can establish firms with AI-enabled capacity rather than relying on the traditional associate-to-partner leverage model. He regards partnership and corporate models as suited to different work and reports hearing UK firms consider corporate subsidiaries for more AI-oriented services. He also argues that high-end partner expertise is currently underpriced and compensated through associate hours, a relationship that AI may reshape. These are strategic observations and expectations, not quantified staffing or employment forecasts.

pts.k: Junestrand presents Portal as a way for firms to offer client self-service AI workflows while retaining the client relationship.
pts.d: He says Portal supports collaboration in both directions but initially focuses on firms offering a white-labelled product to clients. In-house demand for tools already used by outside counsel is his stated commercial basis; his own experience of lengthy fundraising email chains supplies the collaboration rationale. He positions reusable workflows, templates and playbooks as a response to hourly-model resistance and potential loss of automatable work. His claim that this is unprecedented is his own product claim, not a demonstrated historical finding.

pts.k: Junestrand says realised AI benefits depend on organisational change, user learning and substantial implementation support, not merely model or product capability.
pts.d: He characterises changes to legal ways of working and business structure as profound and says enterprise implementation requires local expertise and assistance. He describes model capability as ahead of products, and products as ahead of users. Legora's deployment of legal engineers, including former practising lawyers, is his example of helping teams redesign work. Legora is described here as a software vendor with implementation services, not as an alternative legal service provider delivering client legal work.

pts.k: Junestrand claims substantial product-development headroom remains even with current models, while perfect one-prompt legal drafting remains distant.
pts.d: Rather than directly establishing whether underlying LLM progress is plateauing, he argues that legal products can still improve through scaffolding, techniques and better application of existing capabilities. He says Legora designs functionality to benefit from stronger underlying models. He explicitly rejects present availability of a perfect share purchase agreement from a simple prompt and expects that outcome to remain a long way off. No capability benchmark or drafting evaluation accompanies these claims.

pts.k: Junestrand claims integrated, designed enterprise suites provide value beyond direct access to a general-purpose LLM.
pts.d: He describes Legora's evolution from a chat-style interface into a suite and argues that enterprise scale, usability and connections between functions create additional capabilities. His examples include connecting tabular review with an assistant and supporting large numbers of users and documents. These are product-design and operating-experience claims, not measured comparisons against firms' internally built systems.

pts.k: Junestrand reports rapid legal-AI demand and vendor growth, but treats global leadership as an ambition rather than endorsing a five-company market forecast.
pts.d: He reports growth from a few customers to over 550 following general availability in October 2024, and from 40 employees to more than 220 during 2025, with more than a doubling planned for the following year. He attributes growth to demand for strong products and implementation partners. He declines to predict the ecosystem five years ahead and says Legora would want to be number one if a top-five market emerged. The five-vendor scenario is the interviewer's question, not Junestrand's prediction. Separately, Junestrand claims competition improves products and companies.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Junestrand's product, customer and implementation experience, supplemented by self-reported company figures and an unspecified pilot result.
pts.d: The six-hours-to-20-minutes example supports the time-saving discussion; customer inbound supports the Portal opportunity; fundraising collaboration supplies a workflow pain point; conversations with legal service leaders support his account of pricing and organisational change. Company growth figures indicate reported commercial adoption, not measured legal-work quality. Predictions about consolidation, competitive winners and the repricing of expertise are argued from these experiences and proposed economic mechanisms. The document supplies no independent study, named benchmark, systematic legal-quality test or quantified employment projection.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present-tense observations concern late 2025; most sector predictions are conditional and lack fixed deadlines.
pts.d: The interview identifies its current period as the fourth quarter of 2025. Adoption and product development are described as current; the staffing expansion plan concerns 2026. More complex automation, consolidation and pricing shifts have no specified endpoint. Alternative fees are conditional on providers wishing to retain automatable work. Perfect prompt-only drafting is described as likely distant. Rapid change motivates quarterly operational planning despite longer-term roadmap initiatives, and Junestrand explicitly avoids a five-year ecosystem forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms, other legal service providers, specialist practitioners, enterprise legal buyers, legal engineers and legal-tech vendors.
pts.d: Firms face pricing, client-retention, acquisition and organisational choices. Specialist practitioners may gain capacity to establish firms; partners may need to price scarce expertise differently as associate-hour economics change. In-house teams and corporate clients may obtain firm-provided self-service workflows and shared collaboration environments. Lawyers need training and workflow support, with legal engineers facilitating adoption. Vendors compete through integrated products and implementation capacity across global enterprise markets. The source does not make a concrete access-to-justice claim or quantify associate job losses.
